metaData.title: Musk Spent $10 Billion to Figure Out One Thing: Not Building a Coding Agent Is a Death Sentence
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article thoroughly argues the core point that model providers must build their own coding agent products to obtain high-quality process supervision data and drive continuous model evolution, while analyzing the data game logic behind the $10 billion partnership between SpaceX and Cursor.
metaData.summary: Using the $10 billion partnership between SpaceX and Cursor as a starting point, the article systematically elaborates on the strategic necessity of coding agent products for model providers. The core argument is that model providers training programming models solely on public code data can only learn 'results' but not 'process' signals. Only by owning their own coding agent products (such as Cursor, Claude Code, Codex) can they collect on-policy data from user interactions, including process supervision signals like prompts, rejections, corrections, and undo actions. This data can then be used through reinforcement learning to continuously improve model performance in real-world programming scenarios. The article supports this argument with evidence including Cursor's 'real-time reinforcement learning' case (iterating model versions every 5 hours), Anthropic using Claude Code interaction data to feed back into training, and DeepSeek's performance decline on real benchmarks. It also points out that this logic applies to the broader agent field, where browser plugins and similar products are essentially data collection devices. Finally, the article analyzes the layout of major domestic model providers in the coding agent space and identifies data ownership as the hidden core point of contention.

mainPoints.point: Model providers must build their own coding agent products to obtain high-quality process supervision data.
mainPoints.explanation: Public code data only contains final results, lacking process signals from user interactions such as prompts, rejections, corrections, and undo actions. These signals can only be generated within the runtime environment of a coding agent product and are the key data source for reinforcement learning process supervision.

mainPoints.point: Building your own product enables on-policy data collection, which distillation and other off-policy methods cannot replace.
mainPoints.explanation: The policy gradient theorem in reinforcement learning requires that optimization samples are ideally generated by the model currently being optimized (on-policy). Distilling other models can only approximate results, not capture internal probability distributions, making it prone to errors when the inference path deviates.

mainPoints.point: Cursor's real-time reinforcement learning case demonstrates the value of the product data flywheel.
mainPoints.explanation: Cursor deploys model checkpoints directly to production, iterating as fast as every 5 hours. Its Tab feature, through online RL, reduced rejection rates by 21% and increased acceptance rates by 28%, proving that even without a base model, product data can be used with RL to create a specialized programming model that surpasses the base model.

mainPoints.point: Model providers without their own coding agent products will be exposed on real benchmarks.
mainPoints.explanation: DeepSeek ranks 9th (70%) on SWE-bench bash only, but only 15% on the more realistic SWE-bench Pro. OpenRouter data shows its token consumption is mainly for casual conversation rather than programming, indicating a lack of real-world programming scenario data support.

mainPoints.point: Data ownership is the core point of contention between model providers and product companies.
mainPoints.explanation: Even after being acquired, Cursor retains the autonomy of its own data flywheel and does not collaborate with xAI on developing new models. When all top model providers build their own products and all top products start training models, the boundary between model companies and product companies is disappearing.

keyQuotes: Without your own coding product, there is no high-quality reinforcement learning data; without high-quality data, you cannot train a truly combat-effective coding model.
For model providers to create truly capable programming models, building their own coding agent product is the only path.

(The biggest challenge in training programming models) is modeling the user. Composer's production environment includes not only the computer executing commands but also the person supervising and guiding it. Simulating a computer is easy; simulating the person using it is very difficult.

For any model provider aspiring to master top-tier code capabilities, establishing their own coding agent product is no longer an optional business route, but the core lifeline to ensure the underlying model can continuously evolve.
Data ownership itself is the most critical hidden game point.
